quotation_candidates.quotation: Stroke Stroke is essentially a disease of the cerebral vasculature in which a failure to supply oxygen to brain cells, which are the most susceptible to ischemic damage, leads to their death. Strokes are comprised of two broad categories: ischemic and hemorrhagic. Ischemic strokes account for approximately 80% of strokes, and hemorrhagic strokes account for the remainder. 138

quotation_candidates.quotation: Transient Ischemic Attack Symptoms of a transient ischemic attack (TIA) include the focal deficits of an ischemic stroke within a clearly vascular distribution, but in the case of TIAs patients return to base-line without noticeable clinical deficits within a few minutes to hours. Previously TIAs were thought to be completely reversible without any cerebral infarction; however as the sensitivity of imaging has improved, small areas of infarct frequently can be seen with TIAs. The causes of TIAs are the same as other forms of ischemic stroke. By definition, the clinical symptoms of TIAs must resolve clinically in less than 24 hours. quotation_candidates.quotation: Cardiac Sources Cardiac dysrhythmias, structural anomalies, and acute infarctions are the usual causes of cardiac emboli. The most common source of an embolism is the left atrium of patients with atrial fibrillation. The usual mechanism of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation is by clot forma-tion in the left atrial appendage. This then breaks off and creates an embolus that can move through the arterial sys-tem. Patients older than 60 years are particularly prone to this type of embolization. quotation_candidates.quotation: Vascular Sources The sources of vascular emboli are usually atheromatous plaques in the walls of the aorta, carotid arteries, or smaller vessels in the cerebral circulation. Platelet activation and the formation of a fibrin clot can occur rapidly. The most com-mon areas affected by the emboli of the vascular system are the same as those affected by cardiac sources of emboli. The most common areas for ulcerated plaques in the cerebral blood supply are the aorta and the proximal internal carotid artery. The plaques in the carotid artery can be visualized by Doppler sonography of the carotid artery system. 138

quotation_candidates.quotation: Paradoxical Sources Congenital atrial septal defects can create the opportunity for emboli to cross from the right-sided (venous) circula-tion to the left-sided (arterial) circulation, an uncommon source of cerebral emboli. One of the most common atrial shunting abnormalities is a pat-ent foramen ovale (PFO; the fetal opening between the right and left sides of the heart). quotation_candidates.quotation: Unknown Sources Thrombi of unknown source often occur in patients with known hypercoagulability syndromes. These syndromes can result from acquired diseases (e.g., lupus anticoagulant and metastatic tumors) or inborn errors of the coagula-tion system (e.g., protein S and C deficiencies). Surgery or medication therapies such as estrogen replacement can induce iatrogenic causes of hypercoagulable states. Even when the patient is known to be in a hypercoagulable state, the source of the emboli may remain unknown. In many patients, the entire workup is unrevealing.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Atherosclerotic plaque formation is greatest at the branching points of major vessels and forms in areas of turbulent flow. Chronic hypertension is a common pre-cursor, and damage to the intimal wall may be followed by lymphocyte infiltration. Foam cells then develop, and the first stage of atherosclerosis is formed. Calcification and narrowing with resultant turbulent flow follow. In this setting of turbulent flow, plaque ulceration can become a site for thrombus formation. If a thrombus forms and is degraded rapidly, a TIA can occur. quotation_candidates.quotation: Lacunar Syndrome A lacunar stroke occurs in one of the perforating branches of the circle of Willis, the middle cerebral artery stem, or the vertebral or basilar arteries. The occlusion of these vessels results from the atherothrombotic or lipohyalinotic blockage of one of these arteries. The development of dis-ease in these arteries correlates closely with the presence of chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular dis-ease. 138,83 These are small vessels, 100 to 300 μm in diam-eter, that branch off the main artery and penetrate into the deep gray or white matter of the cerebrum. 20 The result-ing infarcts are from 2 mm to 3 cm in size and account for roughly 20% of all strokes. quotation_candidates.quotation: Hypertensive Bleed Hypertensive cerebral hemorrhages usually occur in one of four sites: the putamen and internal capsule, pons, thalamus, and cerebellum. quotation_candidates.quotation: Arteriovenous Malformation AVMs are found throughout the body and can occur in any part of the brain. The larger AVMs in the brain tend to be found in the posterior portions of the cerebral hemispheres. 42 AVMs occur more fre-quently in men, and if found in one family member, they have a tendency to be found in other members. quotation_candidates.quotation: Posttraumatic Hemorrhagic Stroke A traumatic brain injury commonly results in hemorrhagic damage to the brain in addition to ischemic and other injuries. The four major types of injury caused by trau-matic brain injury include SAH and ICH, diffuse axonal injury, contusions, and anoxic injury from hypoperfusion (decreased flow in the vessels) and hypoxemia (decreased oxygen level). This combination of injuries leads to a con-stellation of findings that mixes the features of a number of individual ischemic and hemorrhagic injuries.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Stroke-like Syndromes A number of conditions in addition to TIAs and cerebral infarctions can cause transient paralysis. These condi-tions generally resolve spontaneously with no long-term sequelae. The most common cause of transient hemipa-resis is Todd paralysis, which develops postictally (after a seizure). Todd paralysis results from neurotransmit-ter depletion and neuronal fatigue in focal areas of the brain caused by the extremely high neuronal firing rate during a seizure. 105 Patients usually regain function within 24 hours. Another common cause of focal neu-rologic deficits is migraine headaches. These headaches are actually thought to result from cerebral vasospasms, but an actual

quotation_candidates.quotation: resolve with the resolution of the migraine and are not permanent. Another common and quickly reversible cause of neurologic deficits is hypoglycemia. One of the first pieces of information obtained when a person is having symptoms suggestive of a stroke is a point of care blood glucose level. If abnormally low, the patient should be given oral or IV dextrose with reassessment of their symptoms.

quotation_candidates.quotation: CT Angiography CT angiography is performed by creating a 3D recon-struction of flow within the blood vessels of the brain after injecting contrast material through a peripheral vein. This helps identify filling defects and any large vessel occlu-sions. As new interventional treatments for acute stroke become more widely accepted, there is a time sensitive need to assess for these large vessel occlusions. When a large vessel is blocked by a thrombus the patient may be eligible for mechanical retrieval of the clot by neuroin-terventionalists. If a large occlusion is suspected, a CT angiogram can be performed immediately after the initial non-contrast CT of the brain.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Magnetic Resonance Imaging MRI is now much more commonly used in acute patients in addition to CT because cost and availability have improved. MRI has the advantage of allowing earlier and more sensitive detection of even small infarcts. Image techniques such as diffusion-weighted imaging help in the identification of early infarcts. 51,157 Magnetic resonance images are created by mapping the relaxation of protons after the imposition of a strong magnetic field. These images are then taken in two primary ways: T1- and T2- weighted images. In T1 images, fat and tissues with simi-lar proton densities are enhanced (bright). In T2 images, water and tissues rich in water are enhanced. As in CT sc

This infor-mation can be used to help determine if the patient might be a candidate for mechanical thrombectomy, even if outside of the usual time window. Despite MRI’s mul-tiple advantages over CT, the rapidity and simplicity of CT imaging has preserved its role as the initial imaging obtained in most cases of suspected acute stroke or ICH. MRI is able to detect the degradation products of hemoglobin (hemosiderin deposits) and show areas of prior hemorrhage well after CT can no longer detect a bleed. The changes on MRI in a chronic infarction are similar to those on a CT scan.

A Holter monitor is a non-invasive device which is worn for 24-48 hours and records ECG activity with external skin elec-trodes. Hospitals that have acute stroke teams, stroke protocols, stroke units and the ability to administer tPA can be certified as Pri-mary Stroke Centers by the Joint Commission. quotation_candidates.quotation: Agents for Cerebral Edema Agents that reduce cerebral edema include corticosteroids, mannitol, glycerol, vinca alkaloids, and piracetam. All the studies done on persons receiving steroids 132 after an acute stroke demonstrated no clear benefits, and steroid use cre-ates a risk of hyperglycemia and DVT. 55 Use of the other agents also has no clear benefit in the treatment of acute stroke, so they are also not routinely used. Interventions for cerebral edema are typically limited to elevating the head of the bed, monitoring serum electrolytes, and neu-rosurgical intervention if cerebral edema is so severe as to necessitate direct reduction of intracranial pressure.

quotation_candidates.quotation: To prevent complications and long-term sequelae after a stroke, maximizing function, decreasing morbidity, and preventing rehospitalization from a complication are important. Many complications are associated with bed rest in general, but some are specific to stroke.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Contractures Contractures are periarticular motion impairments that result from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues, which include muscles, tendons, and ligaments. Con-tractures can occur in any immobilized joint but are particularly prevalent in paretic limbs after a stroke. In fact, only 10% of hemiplegic stroke patients recover limb strength and mobility rapidly enough to avoid devel-oping contractures 65 Shoulder pain, contractures, and muscle pain occur in 70% to 80% of patients who have had a hemiplegic stroke. 9 Chapter 20 addresses the man-agement and related issues of the hemiplegic shoulder. quotation_candidates.quotation: Osteoporosis Bone is a metabolically active tissue normally in a state of equilibrium between active bone resorption and deposi-tion. The ratio of bone formation to bone resorption is influenced by the stressors to which the bone is subjected, a relationship known as Wolff’s law. 135 The lack of weight bearing and normal stress on long bones on the hemiple-gic side of a stroke patient leads to a predominance of bone resorption. This loss of bone mass can start as early as 30 hours after the beginning of immobility 170 and with bed rest can be as high as 25% to 45% in 30 to 36 weeks. 34 In patients who have had a stroke, osteoporosis is often worse, and the rate of hip fracture is far higher

quotation_candidates.quotation: Falls Falls are of particular concern in survivors of stroke. These patients are at increased risk of hip fracture because of developed osteoporosis, and the acuity of their balance, visual perceptions, and spatial perceptions are decreased. The increased risk of falls has been documented in several studies and is greater in patients who have had a right hemi-spheric stroke. 130,117,128 Fall prevention should emphasize balance and cognitive training, removing environmental hazards, and using adaptive devices. (These measures are reviewed in Chapters 6, 17, 18, 19, 26, and 30.)

When hydrocephalus is suspected, one should perform a CT scan promptly, demonstrated ventricular enlargement in this condition. Treatment typ-ically involves surgical placement of a ventricular shunt. The procedure is well tolerated and can lead to resolu-tion of all the symptoms of hydrocephalus if performed promptly. quotation_candidates.quotation: Post Stroke Pain Pain following a stroke can be secondary to musculoskele-tal, mechanical complications as discussed previously or as a result of damage to the central nervous system. Central pain from a stroke typically presents 1-2 months after the event with burning, tingling, radiating pain. This type of pain affects approximately 10% of stroke survivors and is most common in patients whose strokes affected areas of the CNS carrying sensory pathways. Post stroke central pain syndrome (PSCPS) is classically described due to thalamic stroke, but can originate from damage to sensory tracts throughout the CNS. The pathophysiology of PSCPS has not been entirely elucidated. Most treatments tar

No single drug is approved to treat CRPS, but a combination of antidepressants, steroids for inflammation, topical anesthetics and systemic analge-sics are used for management. quotation_candidates.quotation: Deconditioning Physiological deconditioning in patients after a stroke results from the acute medical illness and the associated bed rest and immobility that may result. Table 1.9 lists some of the effects of deconditioning. All of these factors can alter the ability of the patient to recover. Therefore, it is important to get the patient out of bed early post- stroke, and to increase activity steadily. Very aggressive early mobilization after stroke (within the first day after stroke) should be avoided due to concern that this may actually contribute to worse outcomes. 8

quotation_candidates.quotation: Psychological Complications Stroke is a major life event and is associated with signifi-cant alterations in the individual’s well-being and inde-pendence. After a stroke, patients may go through the four stages of bereavement described by Worden. 85 These include accepting the loss, experienc-ing the pain of the loss, adjusting to a new environment in which previous abilities are missing, and investing in new activities. quotation_candidates.quotation: Skin Breakdown and Decubitus Ulcers Pressure ulcer formation is a serious health problem in debilitated and immobilized patients. After a stroke, patients are at particular risk for pressure ulcers because they have numerous factors contributing to skin break-down. Abnormal sensation, contracture, malnutrition, immobility, and muscle and soft- tissue atrophy often develop and may be complicated by advanced age. Pre-vention of pressure ulcers should be the focus of care. quotation_candidates.quotation: Dysphagia Swallowing disorders are common after a stroke. Dyspha-gia is more common in elderly patients, with an incidence of 25% to 45%. 52,54 Aspiration can lead to pneumonia, and decreased oral intake can lead to dehydration and malnutrition. quotation_candidates.quotation: Deep Venous Thrombosis DVT is a common prob-lem after stroke and has an inci-dence of 23% to 75% depending on the severity of the stroke. Most of the morbidity and mortality associated with DVT results from venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pulmonary embolism (PE) after stroke has an incidence of 10% to 29% and a mortality rate of 10%. 13 The forma-tion of DVT is caused by the triad of risk factors outlined by Virchow postulates: altered blood flow, damage to the blood vessel wall, and altered blood coagulability. Box 1.3 lists the common risk factors for DVT. Of the risk fac-tors for DVT, stasis is one of the most important. After a stroke, DVT is 10 times more common in the paretic leg. 177 DV

quotation_candidates.quotation: The neuro-ICU may be the starting point of occupational therapy (OT) evaluation and treatment. Many patients are evaluated by an occupational therapist within 48 hours of a stroke. The ICU environment is often fast paced with the focus on monitoring the individual patient’s medical status. The primary goals of any neuro-ICU are to stabilize the patient medically, progress the patient neurologically, and support the patient and family through this neurologic crisis. 161 Medical testing and procedures take precedence over any OT treatment. Scheduling OT services may be difficult, treatments may be interrupted, and flexibility is necessary.

quotation_candidates.quotation: External Ventricular Drain The external ventricular drain (EVD) is a small tube sur-gically inserted into the ventricles of the brain, which drains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (Fig. 1.12). The tube is connected to a device that measures the amount of this fluid. This procedure is used when the ICP is elevated, and the drain may be clamped for short periods of time by nursing only. Because of specific calibration, function of the drain, and accuracy in measurement, the head of the bed must be elevated to a specific level. Unless the drain is clamped, the head of the bed may not be changed, and patients should not be mobilized.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Spinal Drain A spinal drain is a catheter placed in the lumbar spine to drain CSF. It can be used for the treatment of CSF leak or to drain excess CSF fluid. The lumbar drain should be set to drain below the level of the leak. When the drain is open and is draining CSF, the spinal drain is set at a determined level next to the bed. At this time, when the drain is opened, patients are placed flat on their backs to allow for drainage. Patients with this drain may get up and out of bed and may engage in ADL treatment only when the drain has been clamped by the nurse. While the drain is open to drain CSF, the patient must remain on bed rest.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Graded Sitting and Standing Activities Supported Sitting in Bed. For the supported sitting in bed position, the head of the bed should gradually be raised in approximately 30- to 40-degree increments to avoid an orthostatic hypotensive response. As the patient tolerates the change in degrees of elevation, the therapist should continue to monitor vital signs. If there appears to be no change in the patient’s blood pressure, the therapist should continue to elevate the head of the bed to approximately 80 degrees. Sit-ting at a slightly reclined position is less taxing on the patient’s energy and requires less recruitment of the neck, trunk, and back musculature to maintain an upright position.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Supported Sitting in a Chair. If the patient is well sup-ported and can endure sitting in a chair at the bedside, “sitting tolerance” or “out of bed tolerance” can be increased. Pillows may be useful at this early stage to sup-port the lumbar spine and weaker upper extremity. When a therapist is placing a pillow under the upper extremity, he or she should make sure the shoulder alignment is in neutral. Adequate postural support may reduce pain and fatigue. The focus of treatment can include but is not lim-ited to the patient performing self-care tasks, visual scan-ning activities, and weight bearing through the upper and lower extremity.

In the ICU, the preferred method for treating edema is positional elevation because compression garments or ace wraps may not be appropriate because of various IVs and line access needed by nursing. leaf_extractions.title: BOX 1.8 Communication Key Points
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management

items.text: • Use a normal tone and volume of voice. Avoid shouting at the patient or talking to the patient in an infantile manner
• Give the patient enough time to respond to the question
• Try to stay on the same subject
• Gesture whenever possible and provide tactile cues as appropriate
• Speak slowly and directly to the patient’s face
• Simplify questions to yes or no
• Try to reduce background noise to eliminate distraction. Close the door and turn off the radio or television
• Only one person should communicate with the patient at one time
• Be aware of signs of frustration by observing facial expressions

leaf_extractions.title: BOX 1.9 Oral Motor Screening
section_path: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management

items.text: • Observe for the presence of facial asymmetry. Facial drooping or weakness is common in association with the weaker extremities. Foods can pocket in the cheek of the weakened side

• Observe mouth and lip closure. Can the patient purse his or her lips? Have him or her attempt to blow air into his or her cheeks while keeping his or her lips pursed. Observe if air escapes through one side of the mouth
• Request the patient to stick out his or her tongue. Does it drift or deviate to one side? Can the patient lick his or her lips and perform lateral movements with the tongue?
• Use a long-­stick swab to assess the patient’s sensation both extra-­ and intraorally
• Use a tongue depressor to assess the patient’s gag reflex. Is it present, absent, or delayed?
• Check the soft palate. Use a flashlight to ask the patient to open mouth and say the word “ah.” Observe for soft palate elevation

• Assess the patient’s vocal quality. Is it gurgly or wet? Can the patient “clear” his or her voice? Secretions may pool or linger around the vocal cords. Is there hoarseness of the voice? If so, it may be due to inadequate closure of the vocal cords
• Can the patient demonstrate a volitional cough? Assess the strength of the cough. Is it adequate to clear the airway?
• Is the patient managing his or her own secretions? Does the patient choke or cough on his or her own secretions? Observe whether the swallow is present or delayed
• A standardized bedside swallowing assessment is recommended (Fig. 1.25)

items.text: • Facial weakness

• Safely moving noncomplex lines and leads. These may be noninvasive such as a blood pressure cuff; an O 2 monitor; an IV line; and, in certain cases, A-­lines.
• Positioning of affected extremities.
• Splint wearing schedule, donning and doffing the splint, and performing skin checks.
• ROM for the elbow, wrist, and hand.

• Setting up environment for patient during ADL tasks supine and interacting with the patient on the affected side (in the case of neglect or sensory loss). As treatment progresses, the family can be further

• Shoulder management: Families must be educated in positioning of the involved upper extremity in bed, dur-ing bed mobility, for transfers, during ADL activities, and while upright. Family members can be instructed to don and doff shoulder supports if needed.

• ADL training: Family members can be trained in setting up the environment using the bedside table, giving simple verbal cues, and providing physical cues to engage the affected upper extremity. If the patient is to go home directly from the acute care setting, family training of both compensatory and remedial techniques for ADL trainings should be initiated.

• Shoulder ROM: After family members are educated on how to safely handle a subluxed shoulder, they can also be educated to passively range the affected shoul-der to 90 degrees of forward flexion. In some cases, occupational therapists can use their clinical judg-ment and teach the family to perform overhead ROM if they can maintain proper alignment of the head of the humerus.

• Positioning: After the family members are edu-cated in upper extremity positioning, they should be involved in the patient’s positioning schedule. A physically able family member should be trained in proper body mechanics during bed positioning. If a family member is unable to physically complete the positioning him-­ or herself, he or she should be educated on the turning schedule and proper posi-tioning. In addition to positioning supine, family
• Transfer training: If a patient is to be discharged from the acute care setting to home transfer, training may be appropriate.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Rehabilitation seeks to help the person with disabilities achieve the highest possible degree of performance. A primary focus in inpatient rehabilitation is indepen-dence in self- care activities. However, some clients may choose to have an attendant help them with basic ADLs for personal, cultural, or other reasons. In such cases, goals can evolve

quotation_candidates.quotation: When a client enters inpatient rehabilitation, an ongoing evaluation of capacities as well as client goals is imperative. Through identification of higher-level tasks, clients can be challenged outside the walls of the rehabilitation hospital. For example, a client walks down the hallway of the hospital. What is the response of the other therapists, nurses, and housekeepers in the hallway? What if 1 week after discharge, that individ-ual is negotiating a shopping mall? Will the persons in the mall have the same response as the hospital staff? Providing rehabilitation in the community rather than restricting it to the hospital setting is the best prepara-tion for life after discharge.

quotation_candidates.quotation: A good outpatient program involves a multidisciplinary team working with the client to achieve maximum inde-pendence in all aspects of life the client indicates as impor-tant. Outpatient therapy forces the client to maintain a schedule of therapies, get ready in time for the appoint-ment, arrange transportation to and from the appoint-ment, and follow through with home programs that are jointly designed with the therapists. It may include help from caregivers. To get to therapy, the client must have the physical endurance to participate in the preparation, the travel, and the therapy itself. The cognitive process involves initiation, planning, attention, organization, and sequencing.

quotation_candidates.quotation: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Describe the motor behavior (i.e., motor control, motor learning, and motor development) theories and model that support the occupational therapy (OT) task-oriented ap-proach to persons after stroke. 2. Describe the evaluation framework for the OT task-oriented approach and identify specific assessments that are con-sistent with the approach. 3. quotation_candidates.quotation: The ecological approach “emphasizes the study of inter-action between the person and the environment during everyday, functional tasks and the close linkage between perception and action (i.e., purposeful movement).” 57 Gib-son described the role of functional goals and the environ-ment in the relationship between perception and action. quotation_candidates.quotation: The study of dynamical systems originated in the disci-plines of mathematics, physics, biology, chemistry, psy-chology, and kinesiology and has been applied to the professions of OT, physical therapy, nursing, adapted physical education, and some areas of medicine. 15,57 Such study has influenced the development of a systems model of motor control as well. Dynamical systems the-ory proposes that behaviors emerge from the interaction of many systems and subsystems. Because the behavior is not specified but is emergent, it is considered to be self-organizing. 48 Despite the many degrees of freedom or ways of performing a task available to persons, they tend to use relatively stable patterns of
quotation_candidates.reference: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 3: Task-Oriented Approach to Stroke Rehabilitation, Dynamical Systems Theory, p. 60–61
quotation_candidates.in_text_citation: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 3, p. 60–61

quotation_candidates.quotation: Explanations of changes in motor behavior in the sys-tems model of motor control are different from earlier reflex-hierarchical models. Thelen 85 stated that an impor-tant characteristic of a system perspective is that the shift from one preferred movement pattern to another is marked by discrete, discontinuous transitions. These changes in only one or several personal or environmental systems (i.e., control parameters) can contribute to transitions in motor behavior. 20 In conclusion, no inherent ordering of systems exists in terms of their influence on motor behavior, and systems themselves are subject to change over time.

leaf_extractions.title: BOX 3.1 Assumptions of the Occupational Therapy Task-Oriented Approach Based on a Systems Model of Motor Behavior
section_path: BOX 3.1 Assumptions of the Occupational Therapy Task-Oriented Approach Based on a Systems Model of Motor Behavior

items.text: • Personal and environmental systems, including the CNS, are heterarchically organized.
• Functional tasks help organize behavior.
• Occupational performance emerges from the interaction of persons and his or her environment.
• Experimentation with various strategies leads to optimal solutions to motor problems.
• Recovery is variable because patient factors and environmental contexts are unique.
• Behavioral changes reflect attempts to compensate and to achieve task performance.

leaf_extractions.title: Experience-Dependent Neural Plasticity

items.text: • Use it or lose it: failure to drive specific brain functions can lead to functional degradation.
• Use it and improve it: training that drives a specific brain function can lead to an enhancement of that function.
• Specificity: the nature of the training experience dic-tates the nature of the plasticity.
• Repetition matters: induction of neural plasticity requires repetition.
• Intensity matters: induction of plasticity requires suf-ficient training intensity.
• Time matters: different forms of plasticity occur dur-ing different times during training.
• Salience matters: the training experience must be suf-ficiently salient to induce plasticity.
• Age matters: training-­induced plasticity occurs more readily in younger brains.
• Transference: plasticity in response to one train-ing experience can enhance the acquisition of similar behaviors.
• Interference: plasticity in response to one experience can interfere with the acquisition of other behaviors. While not explicitly stated, many of the treatment

He was admitted to the acute care hospital and was then transferred to the rehabilitation unit today. From the chart, it was learned that he is now medi-cally stable. He is taking angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors for high blood pressure and Coumadin for pre-vention of a second stroke. leaf_extractions.title: Specific Task-Related Actions That Most Reflect Diminished Quality of Activity of Daily Living Task Performance
section_path: Enhancing Performance of Activities of Daily Living Tasks
Specific Task-Related Actions That Most Reflect Diminished Quality of Activity of Daily Living Task Performance

items.text: • Moves, Transports: Astrid demonstrated moderate to marked physical effort moving her wheelchair, resulting in moderate inefficiency transporting task objects to her workspace (i.e., she was only able to transport one object at a time).

• Aligns, Positions, Reaches, Bends: Astrid consistently leaned far back in her wheelchair and often positioned her-self with her left side toward the kitchen counter, resulting in moderate increase in physical effort when reaching for task objects with her right arm or when bending forward and reaching with her left arm into the refrigerator or cupboards.

• Grips, Manipulates, Coordinates: While stabilizing task objects in her left hand (e.g., bag of oats, tomato, jar), Astrid occasionally fumbled task objects and was unable to firmly grasp task objects held in her right hand (e.g., cup used to scoop oats, knife used to slice tomato, jar lid), resulting in task objects slipping from her right hand and the need for assistance to open a jar of juice.
• Coordinates, Handles: Astrid did not always stabilize task objects, resulting in several task objects almost falling into her lap or onto the floor, including a hot pan of oatmeal.

• Heeds, Chooses: When preparing oatmeal and juice, Astrid chose orange juice instead of the lingonberry juice she had prespecified that she would choose; when making a sandwich, she prepared her sandwich with tomato instead of the cucum-ber she said she would use.

items.text: • Compensatory model: The planning and implementa-tion of adaptive occupations that involve practicing and learning to perform daily life tasks using adapted equipment, assistive technology, compensatory strat-egies, modifications to the physical environment, or modifications to the social environment (e.g., provision of verbal or physical assistance) include using consulta-tive OT services designed to inform clients about (1) the availability of adaptive equipment or (2) what types of adaptations are recommended but then practicing using them independently (e.g., via a home program) or under the supervision of others (e.g., support staff) (Fig. 5.­5). Adaptive occupation is occupation based because the person and others in the client’s constel-lation practice and learn new methods for task perfor-mance in the natural context of performing those daily life tasks. 13

• Educational models: The planning and implementation of educational programs (i.e., lectures, workshops, in-­ services) for groups of clients (e.g., a group of patients, a group of comfort home support staff, a group of com-munity leaders) that maintain a focus on learning about aspects of performance of daily life tasks (Fig. 5.­6).

• Acquisitional models: The planning and implementation of acquisitional occupations in the form of occupational skills training focused on the client reacquiring, devel-oping, or maintaining occupational skill in the context of performing targeted daily life tasks (e.g., practic-ing and learning to transport task objects in the con-text of making sandwiches, practicing and learning to effectively prepare oatmeal in the context of preparing oatmeal) (Fig. 5.­7). Acquisitional models are occupa-tion based because the client is engaged in performing

• Restorative models: The planning and implementation of restorative occupations focused on the client restoring, developing, or maintaining person factors or underly-ing body functions in the context of performing rele-vant daily life tasks (e.g., increasing grip strength in the context of performing simple meal preparation tasks that require the use of the affected hand to grasp task objects, maintaining memory through engaging in card games that require the use of memory) (see Fig. 5.­7). Restorative occupation is occupation based because the client is engaged in meaningful occupation, but it is never occupation focused because the proximal or immediate intended outcome is improved person fac-tors or body functions (e.g., grip strength, memory). 13 As Maria considered which models of practice to choose, she recalled both what she knew about Astrid and the suggestions available in the AMPS manual regarding what approaches might be most effective with clients who have differing levels of ADL motor and ADL process abil-ity. For example, Maria was aware that Astrid’s previous occupational therapist had reported that Astrid’s cognitive limitations limited her ability to learn new, compensa-tory strategies, but Maria did not know if Astrid’s former occupational therapist was referring specifically to learn-ing compensatory or other types of adaptive strategies. She also was aware that, according to the suggestions in the AMPS manual, 16 when a client’s ADL process ability mea-sure is at or below 0.0 logits, he or she may more readily benefit from adaptive strategies based on the provision of structured supports or assistance from others than adaptive occupation that emphasizes learning new compensatory strategies; Astrid’s ADL process measure was 0.0 logits. Moreover, Astrid’s low ADL motor and ADL process abil-ity measures may indicate that Astrid has limited potential to relearn occupational skill through occupational skills training based on the acquisitional model. Finally, Maria was aware that these guidelines from the AMPS manual are based on a “review of the literature and clinical experi-ence. Thus, each occupational therapist must base his or her own decisions on the available evidence supporting cost-­effective improvements of occupational performance in relation to the clients with which he or she works.” 16 Based on this information, Maria decided to try using both acquisitional occupational skills training and intro-ducing compensatory and other adaptive strategies (e.g., adapted equipment), but she reasoned that she would do so cautiously and carefully monitor Astrid’s progress to be sure she benefited from either or both. Maria believed that the use of restorative occupation was not appropriate, partly because she knew that Astrid and her physical ther-apist were focusing on Astrid’s shoulder mobility, postural control, and ability to walk using her rolling walker and partly because she reasoned that Astrid was unlikely to regain much more underlying functions in her right arm or hand. Finally, Maria reasoned that if there was a need to provide an in-­service for the staff at the comfort liv-ing complex, she might try to arrange a session with them where she could orient them to more effective strategies to use to help residents like Astrid. Maria’s next step was to consider Astrid’s goal related to simple meal preparation and then each of her subgoals. She developed the following preliminary ideas for an intervention plan that she planned to discuss with Astrid in order to gather any ideas that Astrid might have, as well as her opinions about how she preferred to proceed with her OT services.

items.text: • In a randomized trial, Sahebalzamani et al. 14 found that stroke patients who received self-­care education performed significantly better than those who did not following discharge from the hospital.

• Legg et al. 11 completed a systematic review and meta-­analysis to determine if OT focused specifically on personal ADLs improves recovery for patients after stroke. Nine RCTs with 1258 participants were included in the analysis. The authors found that this intervention significantly improved ADL performance scores and reduced the risk of a poor outcome.

• Steultjens et al. 16 conducted a systematic review to determine the effectiveness of OT interventions in improving outcomes for stroke patients. The authors reviewed 32 studies, including 18 RCTs. They found that comprehensive OT had a significant impact on primary ADLs, extended ADLs, and social participation.

• Trombly and Ma 17 reviewed 15 studies that included 895 participants; 11 of these studies, including 7 RCTs, found that training led to a significant improvement in role participation and ADL performance. The authors concluded that “occupational therapy effectively improves participation and activity after stroke and recommend that therapists use structured instruction in specific, client-­identified activities, appropriate adaptations to enable performance, practice within a familiar context, and feedback to improve client performance.”

leaf_extractions.title: Showering and Bathing
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • A handheld shower head with control of water flow (https://www.ncmedical.com/item_386.html#!pretty Photo) can help prevent scalding and make it easier to rinse soap and shampoo.
• Place toiletries within easy reach so that they can be safely accessed. Hooks can be installed so that the shower head and other supplies can be accessed with-out difficulty.
• Pump bottles can be used for liquid soap and shampoo to make it easier to use one hand.

• Long-handled sponges or loofahs can increase ease and safety with washing. A sponge with a curved or flex-ible handle (Fig. 6.­4A) (https://www.alimed.com/etac-­ back-­washer.html) can bend in any direction to wash difficult to reach areas such as the back, stronger arm, axilla, and shoulder.

• A bar of soap can be placed inside of a soaper sponge to enable washing without needing to hold a slippery bar of soap. “Soap on a rope” can be made by using a corkscrew to form a hole in the bar of soap and then rope can be threaded through the hole. Alternatively, soap can be placed in knee-­high pantyhose and tied to the shower seat. 7 A wash mitt with a pocket to hold soap can encourage the use of the weaker arm during bathing (Fig. 6.­4B).

• A lightweight towel or terry cloth bathrobe can be used to save energy when drying. To dry the back and stronger arm, the patient can place the towel over the shoulder and reach behind the back to grasp the other end. The towel can then be pulled across the back.

leaf_extractions.title: Washing at the Sink or in Bed
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis
Washing at the Sink or in Bed

items.text: • If the patient is unable to access the bath or shower due to impaired mobility or other safety concerns, bath-ing can be performed seated at the sink. The weaker arm and axilla can be placed in the sink basin for easier access and washed with the stronger side. The unaf-fected arm can be washed by placing a soapy washcloth over the edge of the sink and rubbing the stronger arm over it. As mentioned above, an adaptive sponge can be used to wash the rest of the body.
• Toenails and feet can be cleaned with a footbrush (Fig. 6.­5A) (https://www.alimed.com/alimed-­deluxe-­foot-­ brushes.html) or The Footmate System (Fig. 6.­5B).

• If the patient does not have the ability to wash up at the sink due to poor postural control or endurance, bathing can be performed in bed. A total-­body, pH-­ balanced cleanser can be used for bathing and inconti-nence care. A no-­rinse shampoo cap may be helpful for washing hair.

leaf_extractions.title: Oral Care
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Aspiration precautions (see Chapter 29) should be considered when performing oral care, and modified techniques should be used if the patient is unable to safely use water when brushing teeth. A suction tooth-brush can be used with a suction unit in order to pre-vent aspiration.

• To apply toothpaste, the toothbrush can be stabi-lized with the weaker arm if possible or it can be sta-bilized between the teeth. A built-­up grip, such as a foam tube, can make it easier to hold the toothbrush with the weaker hand. Flip-­top toothpaste bottles or a toothpaste dispenser may make toothpaste application more efficient.
• An electric toothbrush can improve ease and effective-ness when brushing teeth, and dental floss picks can make one-­handed flossing easier. A Waterpik water flosser can also be considered.

• Dentures can be soaked overnight in a mild denture cleaning solution, as recommended by the patient’s den-tist. A suction denture brush may help with one-­handed cleaning. A towel can be placed on the counter or in the sink so that the dentures do not break if dropped.

items.text: • Hairstyle is a personal and individualized choice. Some individuals with hemiparesis may find shorter, low-­ maintenance hairstyles easier to manage.

• Long-­handled hair brushes or combs may help some patients use their weaker arm when styling hair. Light-weight splinting material or foam tubes can also be used to increase grip size and extend handles of favorite grooming tools.

• Hands-­free hair dryer stands or wall mounts are com-mercially available and can leave the unaffected arm free to style hair. A position-­adjustable hair dryer can also be devised using a lightweight blow dryer, a desk lamp with spring-­ balanced arms, a tension control knob at each joint, and a mounting bracket. 4 Hair dryer attachments can also help with hair styling.

leaf_extractions.title: Nail Care
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Nail care should be performed regularly for hygiene and skin integrity and must also be completed with caution. The individual’s sensory, motor, visual, cog-nitive, and perceptual abilities as well as the condition of the nails should all be considered to ensure safety and prevent injury. All nail care should be performed with good lighting and postural support with the upper extremities in a supported position.

• Nail care of the weaker hand can be performed with the hand supported on a table. If the weaker hand has significant spasticity that causes the fingers to curl in, a resting hand splint or other positioning device may be needed to keep the hand open.
• Fingernails of the unaffected hand can be cleaned using a nail brush with suction cups.

• Press-­On One Handed Nail Clipper can help indi-viduals clip the nails of the unaffected hand. With this device, fingernails are inserted into the clipper, and the jaws of the clipper close when the lever is pressed (Fig. 6.­6A).
• The ClipDifferent Nail clipper is an automatic finger-nail clipper that gently trims fingernails via one-­handed push-­button operation (Fig. 6.­6B).
• If the individual has some use of the weaker hand, a nail clipper board with suction feet can be attached to the table and used to clip the nails of the unaffected hand (Fig. 6.­6C).
• A suction emery board can be helpful for filing the nails of the unaffected hand. A normal emery board or sand-paper can also be glued to a piece of wood or taped to a table to stabilize it.

• Nail polish can be applied to the unaffected hand by mounting a clothespin on a piece of wood with a C-­clamp to hold the polish brush. The polish is applied when the nail is moved in relation to the brush.

• Some patients will need a caregiver or podiatrist to clip their toenails due to a variety of safety concerns. Toe-nails are most easily accessed with the foot crossed over the knee or with the feet supported in bed. For patients with difficult lifting their legs or bending, a pistol-­ grip toenail clipper may be helpful if vision and safety awareness are intact and there are no sensory deficits in the feet. An emery board can be attached to splinting material to create a long handle that can be used to file toenails.

leaf_extractions.title: Toileting
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • A toilet paper dispenser should be mounted within easy reach of the unaffected side to allow for one-­handed retrieval with minimal reaching or twisting. Moist wipes can be used in place of toilet paper and might be preferable for patients with incontinence.

• Another option for hygiene is a bidet. Attachments can affix to the toilet seat to assist with cleaning and dry-ing after toileting. These items are both commercially available and can be found through medical supply companies.

• The Feminal is another option for women who require adapted toileting. It is designed so that a woman can urinate in a reclined, seated, or standing position. When gently pressed against the body, the shape cre-ates a leak-­proof seal (Fig. 6.­7).
• For female patients who require catheterization after a stroke, self-­catheterization mirrors are useful in keep-ing the legs spread apart as well as providing a better viewing angle.

leaf_extractions.title: General Principles
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Allow for adequate time and rest breaks.
• Set up the task to allow for success without excessive effort.
• Use loose-­fitting clothing with limited fasteners, such as elastic pants or shorts, during initial training.
• Personal style is important. Gaining techniques and suc-cesses can help the person find out what types of adapta-tions will be needed to wear styles that they enjoy.
• Hemiparetic clothing management can be challenging and awkward at first. Ensure safety by setting up the task with correct positioning from the beginning.
• Focus on the benefits of practice over time to encour-age the patient to build new routines.

items.text: • Before starting training in hemiparetic dressing tech-niques, optimal positioning should be considered. The patient should be seated in a stable chair with both feet placed firmly on the floor to create a solid base of sup-port and improve postural stability.
• In hospital settings, dressing may be initiated in the hospital bed with the head of the bed elevated or with the bed in a chair position.
• If the patient has poor trunk control or impaired sitting balance, the trunk should be firmly supported against the backrest of a chair to ensure stability.

leaf_extractions.title: Fasteners
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Try larger buttons or hooks. A ring or loop can be added to the zipper tab to make it easier to pull zippers up and down.

• A favorite shirt with buttons can be altered by removing the buttons and sewing them onto the outside button holes. Velcro can then be sewn over the inside button holes so that the shirt can be easily closed.

• Regular zippers are quite difficult to fasten with one hand. To wear this type of clothing, the zipper can be kept fastened at the bottom, and the garment can be donned overhead, provided that it is big enough. A large safety pin can be placed at the bottom of the zip-per to prevent the zipper from detaching.

• Magnetic fasteners used in adaptive clothing can make dressing much easier. Patients with implanted medical devices such as pacemakers should consult with their doctors before using these garments as magnets can interfere with such devices.

• Adaptive garments from online retailers use hidden magnetic and Velcro closures with decorative but-tons on the outside to maintain a normal appearance. Clothing with magnetic zippers allows for one-­handed fastening and can now be purchased from brands such as Tommy Hilfiger’s Tommy Adaptive clothing line (https://usa.tommy.com/en/tommy-­adaptive).

leaf_extractions.title: Bras
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Bras should be donned by putting the affected arm in first. Elastic pullover bras, such as sports bras, or front-­ fastening bras are easier to manage than bras that fasten in the back.

• Depending on the elasticity of the bra, back-­fastening bras may be clasped first and then pulled on overhead. Bra extenders can be purchased to make donning easier by increasing the circumference. Bra fasteners can be substituted with larger hooks or a Velcro strap with a D-­ring.

• A back-­fastening bra can be donned by clipping the back strap of the bra to the front of the underwear using a clothes pin. The bra is moved around the torso to fas-ten it in the front. The bra can then be twisted around the waist into the correct position. Place the weaker arm in the strap first and then the stronger arm. 19
• A Buckingham Bra-­Angel (Fig. 6.­9) may be helpful for some patients and uses a technique similar to the one described earlier.

leaf_extractions.title: Shoes
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • To don shoes, the weaker leg can be crossed over the stron-ger leg or a foot stool can be used to elevate the foot, mak-ing it easier to reach. Open the shoe wide to slide the foot into it. A shoe horn may help to slide the heel into the shoe. Alternatively, a small piece of splinting material can be molded to fit around the heel of the shoe so that the back of the shoe does not buckle when the heel is slid into it.

• There are a number of different types of adaptive shoe closures. Adaptive shoes with Velcro, zippers, or elas-tic shoelaces are easier to manage with one hand. Lock Laces are elastic laces that are held in place with a cinch so they do not come loose (Fig. 6.­13).
• Shoes can also be tied using a one-­handed technique, which can be found in resources such as the Occupa-tional Therapy Toolkit™. 7

leaf_extractions.title: Lower Extremity Orthotics
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Lower extremity orthotics can be difficult to manage with one hand, and some patients may need assistance. Orthotics may be easier for some people to don if placed in the shoe first.

• Pants with wide legs or openings at the ankles can make is easier to take orthotics on and off. Adaptive pants with openings at the outside seam that are closed with Velcro, zippers, or magnetic fasteners are available online from retailers such as Tommy Adaptive.
• The Original AFO Assist may be helpful to some patients who have difficulty donning their ankle foot orthosis (Fig. 6.­14) (https://afoassist.com/).

leaf_extractions.title: General Tips
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Use labor-­saving equipment. Many countertop kitchen appliances are available that have easy-­to-­operate but-tons or switches.
• Avoid complicated procedures. Food preparation can be completed in stages such as prechopping vegeta-bles or marinating meat prior to cooking. Use ready-­ prepared foods when possible.
• Oven rack guards can be used to prevent burns when taking items in or out of the oven.
• A toaster oven or microwave placed on an accessible countertop can make it easier to prepare simple hot meals.
• Use lightweight pots and pans to avoid heavy lifting.

leaf_extractions.title: Stabilization
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Dycem can be used to help stabilize items while pre-paring foods and can provide extra grip while opening difficult containers.
• Automatic jar openers are designed to open jars of all sizes.
• Cardboard boxes can be opened by stabilizing the box in a drawer and then carefully slitting the box top open using a scissor or knife with the unaffected extremity.
• Pan holders stabilize pots and pans on a range top while the individual stirs or sautés in order to prevent spillage of hot food (Fig. 6.­15).
• Suction plates and bowls can secure to smooth sur-faces for one-­handed food prep as well as feeding tasks.
• Suction-­bottom brushes can be useful during meal prep-aration to clean fruits and vegetables.
• A jug kettle tipper may increase ease of pouring bev-erages (https://mobiliexpert.com/en/jug-­kettle-­tipper. html).

leaf_extractions.title: Cutting
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Purchase vegetables that come precut.
• Use a pizza slicer to cut softer foods.
• A food processor or a box grater with rubber along the bottom can be used for slicing or grating foods.
• Clamp-­on peelers can be affixed to the countertop in order to peel fruits or vegetables one handed.
• A baggy rack can be used to hold open zip-­lock bags when filling them.

• Cutting boards designed for one-­ handed use come equipped with rubber suction feet to secure the board in place. Stainless steel nails hold food in place for cut-ting and chopping. Food guards keep food from sliding while the individual spreads butter or other condiments (Fig. 6.16).

leaf_extractions.title: Clean Up
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Silicone cooking utensils and bakeware are easy to clean and make the cleanup process quicker.
• Oven-­to-­table cookware cuts down on the number of dishes used.
• Pots and pans can be stabilized for scrubbing by posi-tioning them on a wet dishcloth in the corner of the sink.
• To wash cups and glasses, the patient can use a brush suctioned to the inside of the sink, such as a suction bottle brush (Fig. 6.­17).

quotation_candidates.quotation: Work simplification methods should be applied in the performance of household tasks. Housework requires a great deal of mobility and necessitates getting into awk-ward positions. Housework can be made easier by remov-ing clutter from the house. Time spent cleaning is cut in half without added clutter. To conserve personal energy and ensure ease of performance, adaptive devices such as lightweight, long-handled, and electronic tools may serve as useful supplements.

leaf_extractions.title: Cleaning the Bathroom
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • A long-­ handled sponge can be used to clean the bathroom.

• In houses with multiple levels, extra cleaning materi-als should be kept on each level to avoid carrying heavy supplies up and down stairs. If needed, items can be transported in an apron with large pockets, or a tote bag.

leaf_extractions.title: Laundry
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Fabrics that are completely machine washable and dry-able limit the need for hand washing, simplifying the laundry process.
• Soaking articles overnight in soap or detergent can minimize effort needed to remove dirt with one hand.
• A washboard can be useful for scrubbing out dirt and stubborn stains.
• Small articles can be rolled in a towel and squeezed to remove excess water. Clothes can be wrung out with one hand.
• Drip-­dry clothes should be placed on a hanger before they are removed from the sink.
• Lightweight steam irons are efficient at removing creases from many materials.
• Most ironing boards are height adjustable so that the individual can sit or stand when using them. Ironing also can be done on the kitchen table or a counter cov-ered with a folded towel or sheet.

leaf_extractions.title: Writing
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Individuals with hemiparesis of the dominant hand can determine if writing is a meaningful occupation. Alternatives to handwriting exist and are often imple-mented even in the absence of a hemiparesis. Treat-ment choices will depend on the individual.

• Universal cuffs and various pen-­and-­pencil grips may be helpful for individuals who have some grip strength in the affected hand. Other devices exist to allow for a more gross grasp of writing tools in the absence of hand control or in the case of increased tone.

• Dominance retraining of the stronger arm is an option for individuals who prefer to continue writing by hand. In order to meet the need for a functional signature, intervention related to writing might focus on signing one’s name legibly.
• Paper can be stabilized using Dycem or a nonslip mat. The affected arm may also be used to stabilize writing materials when using the stronger arm to write.

leaf_extractions.title: Using the Telephone
section_path: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis

items.text: • Most smartphones have touch screens and should be relatively easy to use with the stronger hand. Potential visual or cognitive impairments may make cell phone use more difficult and should also be considered.

• Most cell phones have settings that can be adapted to make the phone more accessible. See individual phone manuals or speak to an employee where the phone was purchased for help setting up. Various accessibility apps may also help.

• Patients may have the ability to hold their phone with the weaker hand if it is stabilized on a table top. For patients with difficulty holding the phone while operat-ing, attachments are available to assist with stabilization such as a PopSocket (https://www.popsockets.com). Cell phone stands can be used if the patient is unable to stabilize the phone with the affected arm.
• For texting and typing on phones, most cell phones come with a talk-­to-­text option.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Energy conservation and work simplification techniques can also be applied to instrumental ADLs (IADLs). Patients can prioritize, organize, and limit work in order to save time and energy. In general, patients should allow increased time for task completion and take frequent, short rest breaks. Work surfaces should be positioned at a height that allows for maximal efficiency to avoid exces-sive reaching and bending. To allow for easy access to supplies, items that are frequently used should be kept on convenient shelves at the front of accessible cupboards and drawers or at the back of the work surface. When pos-sible, patients should sit while working to save energy.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Analysis of Movement In the functional mobility task of bridging, the back and hip extensors support the body against the forces of gravity. The arch formed when the upper back and feet are in contact with the supporting surface is maintained by the activation of muscles located on the underside of the arch. Use of the arms or legs increases the demands placed on the trunk muscula-ture. When an arm or leg is raised (as in attempts to dress), the muscles located above the arch (the oblique abdominal muscles) must become active to support the limb. 27

quotation_candidates.quotation: Analysis of Movement The transitional movement from supine to sit may be achieved through a variety of movement strategies. Adults have a tendency to use a momentum strategy to achieve the goal (Fig. 7.10). Their movements are smooth and efficient as they “bound” out of bed, off the couch, or out of a chair. A momentum strategy requires forces within the trunk to be generated and transferred to the lower extremities to initiate the rolling sequence.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Selected Problems As mentioned in the previous section, patients may have difficulty maintaining their feet flat on the floor because of poor sensation, unilateral inattention, or shortening of the trunk and calf muscles. Difficulties with spatial relations and praxis have been noted during transfer training, regardless of whether the therapist is training the patient for pivot transfers or sit to stand. Certain patients lean backward instead of for-ward while the therapist is attempting to transfer. These patients’ actions are unpredictable and often run counter to those expected after instruction from the therapist.

quotation_candidates.quotation: As Árnadóttir 6 noted, transfers also reveal problems with organizing and sequencing and conditions such as ideational apraxia. quotation_candidates.quotation: The ability to stand is a goal many patients with hemi-plegia want to achieve because the drive to be upright is strong. Patients should be provided the opportunity to practice standing and shifting their centers of gravity in all directions and reaching for functional objects in the environment. The trunk responses needed for controlled sitting (i.e., selective lengthening and shortening depend-ing on the requirements of the task) also are needed for controlled standing; however, these trunk responses are carried out over a much narrower base of support.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Standing may prove challenging for patients with severe hemiplegia who have only one side of the body available to use for movement; moving with one half of the body is stressful work. The slow, laborious effort of standing and attempting to move in this position causes an increase in posturing and skeletal muscle activity. Movements often are lacking in spontaneity and must occur at a conscious level for the patient. Postural deviations noted in sitting in these patients become even more exaggerated in standing. For example, a patient who tends to “fix” the upper limb to stay upright while sitting will present with greater fixa-tion of the upper limb when challenged in the standing position

quotation_candidates.quotation: Patients rely on feedback for performance of all mobility tasks. For example, before initiating a transfer, a patient uses visual information about the appropriate position of the limbs before movement begins. As the patient begins to rise from the seated position, the somatosensory system pro-vides information about the forces exerted and the ongoing changes in limb position. On completion of this task, the results of the sequence provide additional feedback. The patient uses the feedback given to gain a sense of how it felt to rise to a standing position. Was it efficient? Was it dif-ficult? This information gained during or after the mobility sequence is termed movement-produced feedback.
quotation_candidates.reference: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Feedback, p. 165–167
quotation_candidates.in_text_citation: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 165–167

quotation_candidates.quotation: Feedback is important to the rehabilitation process, and the therapist should carefully select the type of feedback provided, the amount, and the schedule. Feed-back should be distinguished from encouragement, which facilitates continued participation of the patient in the mobility task. “Try more” and “Keep going!” are examples of encouragement that recognize the patient’s effort. Forms of feedback for coming to the stand posi-tion include: “Good job. You were able to stand at the sink” (knowledge of results [KR]) or “Next time you need to lean forward more before rising” (knowl-edge of performance [KP]). leaf_extractions.visual_policy: Tables are referenced as reconstructed table records; non-table visuals retain location/name only.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Early in the treatment process, most functional mobil-ity tasks may be considered closed, and the environmen-tal features are regulated easily to improve performance. Rolling over and coming to a seated position in a hospi-tal bed occurs on a stationary surface. The therapist can regulate the environment further by positioning pillows and bed linens appropriately, raising the bed guard rails, adjusting the height of the bed, limiting the number of persons moving around the patient’s bed, and position-ing the body in a fairly static position to assist the patient if needed. Another important characteristic of a closed
quotation_candidates.reference: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Closed Tasks, p. 171
quotation_candidates.in_text_citation: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 171

quotation_candidates.quotation: task is that movement is self-paced, and no temporal con-straints are placed. The therapist’s role as a regulator can be equated with the degree of assistance or handling provided. The thera-pist initially may give significant physical assistance and use a variety of adjunct techniques to promote perceptual, cognitive, and sensory processing. As the patient regains control of movements in desired sequences, physical assis-tance and the amount of cueing are reduced gradually or eliminated. 72

quotation_candidates.quotation: Bed mobility becomes a variable motionless task if the therapist is not present to regulate certain features of the environment. Patients preparing to get out of bed inde-pendently may find the pillows and bed linens in disar-ray, making movement difficult; the bed guard rails are lowered, the top of the bed remains slightly elevated, and the height of the bed may be too high. Simultaneously, the patient may be receiving verbal encouragement to “hurry up.” Without the therapist present to structure the envi-ronment, the patient may experience difficulty and may use compensatory strategies incompatible with the res-toration of performance component deficits. quotation_candidates.quotation: Many advanced mobility skills meet the criterion of an open task in which the spatial and temporal parameters of movement are determined by events occurring in the envi-ronment. Open tasks require more precise timing of move-ment, and the patient is challenged to anticipate and react to unexpected events. A sit-to-stand maneuver on a moving train, plane, or bus is an example of an open task. Practice of this kind of task should occur in the actual environment whenever possible. 44,72 Patients who are physically capable of attempting these advanced skills should be engaged in them while in the rehabilitation setting whenever possible. leaf_extractions.title: Rolling

items.text: • Practice rolling on a narrow surface such as a sofa.
• Encourage abrupt change in direction, as in reversing the movement in midstream.
• Practice rolling under a heavy quilt.
• Try rolling with an object such as a newspaper in the hand.
• Attempt propping to side lying to adjust pillows.
• Practice rolling in a darkened room.
• Ask the patient to roll quickly.

quotation_candidates.quotation: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand typical gait components. 2. Identify common gait deviations after a stroke. 3. Understand the basics of gait retraining, including common outcome measures used to demonstrate improvement. 4. Describe the relationship of bone mineral density to ambulation function after a stroke. 5. Examine the pathologic and impairment evidence along with the therapeutic suggestions for individuals who demonstrate contraversive pushing. 6. Identify and describe commonly used orthoses and assistive devices.

quotation_candidates.quotation: The type of gait of a person who has had a stroke depends on where in the brain the insult has occurred and which systems are affected, such as motor, sensory, balance, coordination, perceptual, and visual systems. If a motor area in the cortex or a motor track is involved, hemiple-gia or hemiparesis is manifested in the contralateral limbs. The location of the infarction within these areas deter-mines whether the arm or the leg is more impaired. Not all patients after stroke are hemiplegic or hemiparetic, nor do all hemiparetic patients have the same degree of motor deficits. quotation_candidates.quotation: A person who has an infarct in the cerebellum caused by occlusion or hemorrhage of a vertebral or a cerebel-lar artery may exhibit completely different gait deviations than a hemiparetic patient. The cerebellum is composed of three parts or lobes: the flocculonodular lobe, the ante-rior lobe, and the posterior lobe. The flocculonodular lobe also is called the vestibulocerebellum because most of its input is from the vestibular nuclei in the pons. The anterior lobe also is known as the spinocerebellum because most of its input is from the spinocerebellar tracts via the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the superior cerebellar peduncle. The posterior lobe also is known as the neocer-ebellum and

quotation_candidates.quotation: or hypotonia in addition to other deficits. These arteries are part of the posterior circulation—the vertebrobasilar system. The posterior inferior cerebellar artery is a branch of the vertebral artery, and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and superior cerebellar artery are branches of the basilar artery. quotation_candidates.quotation: An unusual motor behavior that patients with hemiple-gia sometimes display in the clinic is ipsilateral pushing. The patients tend to push away from the unaffected side in any position. Davies 34 described the syndrome in 1985 and called it the pusher syndrome. The original description of the pusher syndrome was based solely on a practitio-ner’s observation and was most often thought to be asso-ciated with left hemiplegia. 34 The behavior was seen in as many as 10% of the 327 patients after stroke in the study by Pedersen and colleagues. 101 However, the syndrome appears in both right and left hemisphere damage. 69,101 Neglect and aphasia are also highly associated with push-ing behavior. 69

quotation_candidates.quotation: An orthosis (from the Greek adjective orthos, meaning “straight”) is an external device that improves a person’s function when applied to a body part. 82 The more com-monly used term for an orthosis is a brace. Orthoses now are named according to the joints they encompass. Short leg braces are known as ankle/foot orthoses (AFOs). A long leg brace is known as a knee/ankle/foot orthosis (KAFO) or a hip/knee/ankle/foot orthosis if it contains a hip joint and a knee joint. The newer terminology is more descriptive and specific and avoids confusion. Orthotic devices are prescribed by a physician and fab-ricated by an orthotist. The physical therapist provides input to the physician and orthotist

quotation_candidates.quotation: The assistive devices most commonly used with patients after stroke are canes, walkers, and occasionally two crutches. Hemiparetic patients whose balance is impaired minimally and who have functional strength in the oppo-site UE may use a cane. Two crutches or a walker requires at least some functional use of both upper extremities. Both devices provide more external stability, with the walker providing more stability than the crutches. The main function of a cane is to increase the base of support and thereby improve balance. 117 The base of support is increased by providing another contact with the floor. quotation_candidates.quotation: Eric is a land surveyor for a small surveying and engineer-ing firm. He experienced a small stroke and was able to return to work; however, only part-time work was avail-able. Several months later, he experienced a second stroke and was seen by OT. The JPM was used to identify the required work tasks, tools used, and common environ-mental conditions encountered. The requirements of his job included ability to walk, climb, and carry tools for extended distances over even and uneven terrain; work in reaching, squatted, and bent positions; prolonged standing; use of a machete to clear brush; operation of a hand-based computer; and the ability to work outdoors in all types of weather conditions.

quotation_candidates.quotation: The generation born between 1945 and 1964 is affection-ately known as the Baby Boomers. News media, politicians, insurance companies, and advertisers have spent significant resources and time researching this generation because the numbers of individuals in the age group overwhelmingly outnumber other cohort groups. Currently, as the Boom-ers move into later stages of adulthood, the unique aspects of this generation will continue to change OT practice over the next several decades. For example, there will be a shift from the Depression-era seniors, fearful to spend too much money on near necessities, to the Boomers, who overspend on luxuries. Teenagers drove to their local gathering places, whether it was a high school sports game, concert, or swimming pool. leaf_extractions.title: Facilitating Physical Care by the Parent
section_path: Facilitating Physical Care by the Parent

items.text: • Holding: The task of holding is a prerequisite for car-rying, transferring, feeding, changing, burping, and comforting a child.

• Carrying and moving: The task of carrying is a prereq-uisite for moving around the house and community. If a caregiver cannot carry or move the baby, then he or she will be confined to functioning in one room.
• Transfers: The task of transfer is a prerequisite to being able to do several activities such as diapering and put-ting the baby into a crib or high chair.

• Positional change: The task of positional change is a prerequisite for being able to burp a baby and diaper change a baby. A positional change is defined as chang-ing a position of the baby while the baby remains on the same surface.

quotation_candidates.quotation: Being able to provide physical care to the baby is one of the essential elements in parenting. For a caregiver who has had a stroke to pursue the dream of caring for a baby, he or she may need baby care equipment, appropriate durable medical equipment (DME), and adaptive tech-niques. Transitional tasks refer to tasks that are necessary before accomplishing or between basic baby care tasks. Therefore, it is important to begin intervention with these tasks: (1) holding, (2) carrying and moving, (3) transfers, and (4) positional change. 12

quotation_candidates.quotation: Transfers Lifting an infant who does not yet have head control can pose a challenge for people with limited upper extremity use. The easiest solution is to use a baby carrier sling (see equipment chart). If the baby does not accept the sling, the following technique can be used while a parent is in a sitting position in order to transfer from lap to surface. (1) Choose or arrange surfaces that are high enough to avoid back strain. (2) Place the functional hand under the baby’s head. (3) Bend over and simultaneously pull the baby to the caregiver’s chest. The chest acts like another arm to support and hold the baby. (4) Straighten up and move the baby. A caregiver can wear a fanny pack stuffe

quotation_candidates.quotation: Bedtime TLG gets more calls about issues with bedtime than any other topic. For most clients, the greatest difficulty occurs in the course of the transfer activity of putting the baby in bed. The parent can often enjoy the ritual of dressing his or her child in night clothes, reading a book, cuddling, and perhaps singing a song, but because most cribs are inac-cessible, the soothing bedtime activities feel incomplete, resulting in frustration for parent and child alike. Some commercially available infant beds allow the child to sleep with the parent, but these have flaws. The Co-Sleeper, which attaches to the adult bed, poses prob-lems for parents with disabilities because it can make it dif

quotation_candidates.quotation: is workable for the parent but not for the child. TLG has used a two-step lock, but this could be difficult for a par-ent who has apraxia or sequencing issues. TLG does not recommend using a top bar to stabilize the sliding door because babies can hit their heads coming out, especially if the baby is already crying and upset. Adaptations of commercially available cribs cause problems to structural integrity; therefore, adapted cribs need to be frequently checked to assure safety (Fig. 11.6).

quotation_candidates.quotation: Childproofing Home visiting is essential to address childproofing. Some childproofing can be adultproofing because devices may be too complicated for a parent because of cognitive and physical difficulty. It is necessary to try several types of devices to see which one is successful. The process is an opportunity to assess visual and visual neglect issues, apraxia, sequencing, and motor planning. See Chapters 24 to 26. It should be noted that access without raised thresh-olds for walkers and wheelchair access needs to be consid-ered when using safety gates.

If a table is used for another activity, it is important to have a diapering surface that can be removed from the table. quotation_candidates.quotation: In diapering a child, application of the parent–child collab-orative technique is essential. Most babies can be “trained” to do the “bottoms-up” technique. Parents can teach their baby to lift his or her bottom by lifting the baby’s bottom with the working arm and saying, “Up, up” simultaneously. With time, many babies will then lift their bottoms when cued with the words “up, up” or “butt up.” With infants who are premature or still mostly in the flexed position, the caregiver can rest the baby’s bottom on the caregiver’s functional palm and lift the child onto the diaper.
